title: Nepal awaits loss and damage fund support after floods - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal awaits loss and damage fund support after floods  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal is awaiting an official response to its request for urgent support from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage after a sudden flood in the Bhote Koshi river basin. The flood occurred on August 26 in the northern district of Rasuwa, damaging settlements, roads and energy infrastructure.

According to Nepali scientist Manjit Dhakal, who advises the least developed countries in the UN climate process, the disaster claimed the lives of more than 1,450 people, while nearly 6,000 others are still considered missing.

The risks were known

Climate Home News editor Megan Rowling noted that the risks associated with accelerated glacier melting in the Himalayas have been studied for decades. At the same time, in her view, this knowledge was not translated quickly enough into practical measures to protect communities.

The publication also recalled previous studies of risks for downstream communities, international programs to prevent glacial lake outburst floods, and attempts to establish monitoring systems. Bill McGuire, former head of the Benfield Hazard Research Centre at University College London, had previously forecast an increase in the number of large-scale landslides in mountainous areas.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Adaptation financing gap

During Climate Week NYC, experts from Nepal, Brazil, Sierra Leone and the Marshall Islands discussed practical adaptation measures. These included planting trees to stabilize slopes, heat insurance for informal workers, drought-resistant seeds and solar panels for irrigating agricultural land along the Nile.

Mikko Ollikainen, head of the UN Adaptation Fund, said that the fund's project portfolio amounts to $1.6 billion, while projects awaiting financing require another $1.8 billion. According to him, donor countries have not met the annual target of raising $300 million at COP climate conferences in recent years.

Julia Gardiner, chair of the UN implementation body, said that at COP31 in Turkey, governments may face pressure to meet the goal of tripling adaptation finance by 2035 and replenish the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. Prakriti Dhakal, personal deputy to the secretary of Nepal's prime minister, called on international partners to turn compassion into long-term support for affected communities, including by supporting Nepal's proposed Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism.

title: Manassas nonprofit delivers $92,964 for Nepal flood relief - Potomac Local News
description: Manassas nonprofit delivers $92,964 for Nepal flood relief  Potomac Local News

full_article:
America Nepal Helping Society in Virginia Raises $92,964 for Nepal Flood and Landslide Relief

167 donors came together through America Nepal Helping Society to support families in the Rasuwa–Bhotekoshi region

MANASSAS, VA — The America Nepal Helping Society (ANHS), a Virginia-based nonprofit serving the America Nepal Helping Society, has raised and delivered $92,964 to support relief and recovery for communities hit by the recent floods and landslides in Nepal’s Rasuwa–Bhotekoshi region.

A delegation from ANHS traveled from Virginia to New York to present the relief check to the Government of Nepal during a meeting with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal, who was in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly. The handover took place at an interaction program hosted by the Consulate General of Nepal in New York.

A community that came together

As soon as news of the Bhotekoshi disaster reached Virginia, ANHS held a candlelight tribute at the NYAC building to honor those who lost their lives and to stand with grieving families. The organization then formed an 11-member relief committee to reach out to members, local organizations, businesses, and individual donors.

The committee was coordinated by Madhusudan Panthi, former chief patron and advisor of ANHS. Members included Kedar Prasad Timalsina, Chair of the Board of Trustees; Kamana Panthy Adhikari, President; former presidents Sagar Kandel, Padam Raj Regmi, Kamala Kharel, Kamal Bhattarai, and Janu Ojha; Finance Chief Tilak Kharel; General Secretary Bishnu Neupane; and Treasurer Dhruba Baral.

In total, 167 donors contributed to the campaign. For ANHS, the gift is about more than money. It is a sign that Nepali-Americans stand with their families and neighbors back home.

“When our homeland faces a crisis, the Nepali community in America stands together to help,” ANHS said. “This campaign reflects our shared responsibility, compassion, and connection between Nepal and the Nepali diaspora.”

Standing with communities in times of need

Founded in Manassas in 2008 and registered as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, ANHS has long connected the America Nepal Helping Society with Nepal through cultural, educational, and humanitarian work.

After the 2015 earthquake in Nepal, ANHS raised funds and supported relief efforts across the country. Since then, the organization has responded whenever major emergencies strike Nepal, and it has also supported people and communities in the United States and elsewhere during difficult times.

Keeping Nepali language and culture alive

Education and cultural preservation are at the heart of ANHS’s work. Since 2016, the organization has offered Nepali language education to children growing up in the United States. Today, more than 270 children of Nepali origin from several states are learning Nepali through ANHS programs.

ANHS has also developed and published its own Nepali-language curriculum, now used by Nepali schools in the United States and abroad. The curriculum has been recognized by Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre, an important step in keeping the language and cultural roots strong among children in the diaspora.

Thank you to everyone who helped

ANHS extends heartfelt thanks to every donor, family, business, volunteer, community organization, and elected official who made this campaign possible.

The organization also offered special thanks to Danica Roem for her support. “Thank you, Danica Roem, for standing with our community,” ANHS representatives said. “We know you are with us, and we are with you. We look forward to your continued partnership.”

ANHS is also grateful to the local media outlets that have kept the Washington region and Virginia informed about the disaster in Nepal and the response of the America Nepal Helping Society, including WTOP, 7News (WJLA / ABC7), NBC4 Washington, InsideNoVA, and 12 On Your Side (NBC12 Richmond). The organization extends special thanks to WTOP and ABC News for their coverage, which helped raise awareness, honor the victims, and encourage support for families in need.

We are with you

ANHS’s message to the community is simple: we are here for you. Whether you are a family in Nepal rebuilding after disaster, a parent who wants your child to learn Nepali, a newcomer to Virginia looking for support, or a neighbor facing a hard time, please reach out. If there is anything you need, let us know. We are with you, and we will stand with you.

###

About America Nepal Helping Society

America Nepal Helping Society (ANHS) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit (EIN 26-4735332) founded in 2008 in Northern Virginia. ANHS promotes Nepali language, culture, arts, and traditions in the United States; runs Nepali language education for children; and provides humanitarian and disaster relief in Nepal and in the United States.

A spokeswoman for the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said at least 15 people have been injured and 11 are still missing since the latest wave of heavy rainfall began on Thursday.

A total of 23 deaths occurred due to landslides, while other causes included floods, avalanche and heavy rainfall, spokeswoman Shanti Mahat added. Nearly 1200 families were affected, with hundreds of houses totally or partially damaged, alongside cowsheds and farmlands.

title: MegaVoice brings Gospel hope to Nepal after disaster - Mission Network News
description: MegaVoice brings Gospel hope to Nepal after disaster  Mission Network News
publisher.title: Mission Network News
full_article:
Nepal (MNN) — A month after Nepal’s glacial mountain collapse, thousands of Nepali people have been confirmed dead. Others are still missing or unidentified .

Natural disasters, including flash flooding, monsoons , landslides , and avalanches, continue to strike the country.

(Photo courtesy of MegaVoice)

Amid chaos and pain on the ground, MegaVoice is partnering with donors to send the hope of the gospel to people in need.

“There are several partners that we’re hearing from on the ground,” Matt Copeland with MegaVoice says. The partners say that there is a “desperate need because of the tragedy that’s just happened for the Word of God to be brought to them, so that they could find peace and hope in the Word through this suffering.”

Donors came together to fund the distribution of audio Bibles and solar-powered lights, or “Life Lights.” These devices do not need electricity, making them especially useful when infrastructure is down.

Copeland says giving people Scripture is as much a critical need as food, water, and shelter.

“At MegaVoice, what we’re directly involved with is providing the Word of God in (people’s) heart languages,” Copeland says. “This is the area that we focus on and can help.”

MegaVoice is hearing from partners on the ground that Nepali people are spiritually seeking.

“Their hearts are open. There’s a hunger for it, and they’re receptive. They’re wanting to hear, and many are receiving,” Copeland says.

Before the disasters, MegaVoice was already working with partners to translate the New Testament into 33 dialects spoken in Nepal for the first time . This crisis shows the importance of the work.

According to Operation World , only 2.9% of the people in the country are believers, and only 55% have ever been evangelized or heard the gospel.

Please pray that out of this tragedy, the Lord would lay on people’s hearts the opportunity to reach those in Nepal.

Ask God for His favor over the translation work. Ask for it to be completed swiftly so that His name is known around the world.

Pray that the Nepali people would hear the gospel and come to a saving relationship with Jesus Christ.

full_article:
Dozens of people were confirmed dead and hundreds more are missing after a flash flood swept through remote valleys in Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday.

Nepali police said that authorities have recovered 157 bodies. Officers were "working to move families in flood-risk areas... to safer locations," police said.

"The pain and loss you have suffered is not small. But I want to assure you that you are not alone in this difficult time — the state is with you with all its means and resources," Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a statement.

"Please be patient. The government takes full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food and shelter. In times of such a disaster, we all need to stand together."

In China, authorities said at least three have died, with 265 still missing, China's state broadcaster CCTV ‌said.

Devastating flash floods hit northern Nepal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The floodwaters washed away villages, damaged bridges and destroyed electrical infrastructure on both sides of the Nepal-China border.

"There is devastation everywhere we look," ‌Tula ​Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa district, told Reuters.

"The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing."

At the same time, Chinese authorities also reported that a mudslide caused "major casualties" on the other side of the border in Tibet.

Security cameras captured the moment a wall of mud hit the Nepal-China border Image: REUTERS

Hundreds of people missing

Nepal's Tourism Ministry said 403 travelers were reported missing for several hours after the floods struck.

Missing travelers included 341 foreign tourists, among them were:

142 people from India

47 from the United States

34 from Australia

33 from Britain

24 from Canada,

At least 62 missing Nepali citizens

Other nationalities of those missing included people from

Malaysia

The Netherlands

Portugal

South Africa

South Korea

China's state news agency Xinhua reported Thursday that the number of missing people had increased to 558. State broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the missing people were foreigners.

The burst river also inundated villages in Dhading district Image: REUTERS

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday that 34 Australians were missing following the flash flooding.

"Our thoughts are with all those who will be concerned about their loved ones today," Albanese said.

A Nepali police spokesperson told Germany's DPA news agency that dozens of personnel were also missing.

"So far, we only have confirmation of 26 police personnel who remain missing in the flood," they said.

"We also have missing information of government revenue officials, hydropower workers among others. But we are still collecting the data."

What caused the flash floods?

Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said an earthquake triggered an avalanche in the Himalayas that then triggered flash floods in the valleys below.

Xinhua said a mudslide on the Nepali side of the mountains spread to Gyirong County in Tibet.

"Entire villages and market areas have been wiped out," said David Fisher, the Nepal head of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

Major rescue operations underway

Nepal dispatched more than a dozen rescue helicopters to the mountainous Rasuwa region, but floodwaters were too high for the helicopters to land.

Nepal's prime minister said the military and police were assisting with rescues.

"Instructions have been given ... to move ​the people living in the lower areas ⁠to safer places," Shah said. "People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert."

Rescue helocopters were initually unable to land due to the high floodwaters Image: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP

Chinese President Xi Jinping also ordered an "all out" rescue effort.

He said "the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people... quickly treat injured people and minimize casualties to the greatest extent possible," according to Chinese state media.

A second flood may be imminent, according to Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," he told the AFP news agency.

title: Opinion | Nepal finally found its voice at the UN - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Nepal finally found its voice at the UN  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Every September, Nepal gets about 15 minutes at the world’s biggest podium, the UN General Assembly. For most of the last decade, our prime ministers used that time the same careful way to praise Nepal’s Himalayan and Buddhist heritage, ask the world for climate justice and development support, and, whatever else is said, avoid naming India and China in the same sentence. However, that habit broke this year. And the reasons why matter for every Nepali, not just diplomats.

Look back at Sher Bahadur Deuba’s 2017 address , delivered as Nepal was still rebuilding after the 2015 earthquake. He spoke of building connectivity ‘with countries on both sides’, never naming India or China, even though everyone in the hall knew exactly who he meant. Pushpa Kamal Dahal’s 2023 speech called Nepal ‘a bridge between two large economies’. KP Sharma Oli’s 2024 statement spoke only of ‘our large neighbours’ while discussing trade and investment, again, never India, never China, by name, together.

Sitting between two giant, nuclear-armed neighbours whose combined economy dwarfs our own, Nepal’s leaders have long treated silence as protection, a way to avoid looking closer to Delhi than Beijing, or the reverse. It has been, in its own way, a form of survival diplomacy.

Then the floods came, and the silence broke. On September 25 this year, Prime Minister Balendra Shah, Nepal’s youngest-ever prime minister, stood at the same podium and did something none of his three predecessors had done. In his full address , he thanked ‘our immediate neighbours, India and China’ by name for helping after catastrophe struck, and proposed a named ‘Himalaya Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China’ to monitor dangerous glacial lakes and coordinate disaster response.

The context explains why. Four weeks earlier, the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods, triggered by a surge that crossed into Nepal from the Tibetan side of the border and swept downstream toward India, became one of the deadliest disasters in Nepal’s modern history. By September 24, Nepal Police had confirmed 1,453 dead and nearly 4,800 still missing across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan.

“Climate change does not recognise borders,” Shah told the Assembly. “Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps on passports.” You cannot ask ‘countries on both sides’ to share satellite data and coordinate rescues. You have to say who you mean.

What makes this more than a one-off is that Shah had already tested this same instinct earlier this year, and it went badly. In late May, he told Parliament that border encroachment was not only India’s fault but Nepal’s too, and revealed Kathmandu had raised the matter with both China and the United Kingdom. India read this as an attempt to internationalise a bilateral dispute , and Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal had to travel to New Delhi weeks later to calm the fallout, insisting Nepal was not seeking outside mediation .

Seen against that episode, Shah’s UN speech looks less like a young leader speaking out of turn, and more like a deliberate correction: the same willingness to name our neighbours, but this time wrapped in gratitude and cooperation instead of grievance. That is a meaningful lesson learned in six months of office, and it deserves to be recognised as such.

Shah’s proposal also lands at a genuinely useful moment. India and China have spent the last two years cautiously rebuilding trust after their 2020 border clash, resuming direct flights, pulling back troops, and, importantly, agreeing this year to restart cooperation on sharing data about rivers that cross their shared border. Nepal is not asking two estranged giants to start from zero. It is asking them to widen a partnership they are already rebuilding, to include the country sitting in the middle of them.

The real test comes in six weeks, when world leaders gather in Türkiye for COP31, the UN’s biggest climate summit, focused this year on adaptation and delivering long-promised climate finance. Nepal should use the opening created by Shah’s speech to press for three concrete things, not vague appeals.

First, turn the Himalaya Climate Resilience Mechanism from a UN speech into a signed agreement before or during Belém; even a modest, technical pilot on glacial-lake monitoring would be more valuable than a grand announcement with no substance behind it.

Second, demand that the Loss and Damage Fund and Global Environment Facility, which Shah correctly called ‘grossly inadequate’, commit specific, fast-disbursing grants, not loans, for mountain nations facing glacial-lake outburst floods, since Nepal cannot afford to borrow its way out of a crisis it did not cause.

Third, push for the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, home to nearly two billion people downstream, to get the same dedicated attention at COP31 that small island states have long received. Nepal should not let its case get lost between the more visible sea-level-rise narrative and its own less-photogenic mountain crisis.

title: Opinion | What Lubra can teach Nepal about climate-induced migration and resettlement - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | What Lubra can teach Nepal about climate-induced migration and resettlement  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
In May 2026, I travelled to Lubra, a village at 2,950 metres in Mustang, for my master’s dissertation fieldwork. I explored how its Indigenous Bon community understands its settlement future. What I found challenged the assumption that climate risk automatically leads to migration.

Lubra is an approximately 800-year-old settlement and home to one of Nepal’s remaining Bon communities. Around 40 people remain across nine households, as environmental hazards, outmigration and population decline shape the village’s uncertain future.

But Lubra is more than a collection of houses on a map. Livelihoods, spirituality, memory and identity are rooted in its landscape. Its monastery, chortens, sacred artefacts, traditional homes and farmland are part of the community’s history and its enduring ties to place.

(Left) The new monastery sustaining Bon religious life in the village. (Right) The oldest Bon monastery, central to community identity/Prakriti Joshi

(Left) Interior of the monastery, where Bon rituals and daily prayers sustain spiritual continuity. (Right) Exterior of the monastery/Prakriti Joshi

That relationship is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain as the climate changes. Residents described warmer winters, less snowfall and shifting rainfall, changes they are experiencing in their fields, water sources and daily lives.

Nowhere is this more visible than in the Panda Khola.

The Panda Khola River, a vital water source and growing hazard in Lubra./Prakriti Joshi

Lower Lubra settlement beside the Panda Khola, where flooding and sediment buildup threaten homes and farmland./Prakriti Joshi

During the monsoon, the narrow Lubra River can swell dramatically, spreading across the valley and carrying sediment, cobbles and large boulders. Residents told me that floods they once experienced every three to five years have, over the past decade, occurred almost every year. Each flood leaves sediment behind. Over time, the riverbed has risen, encroaching on the village and burying agricultural land. Research estimates that it has risen by around 12 metres over the last decade, increasing exposure to homes and community infrastructure.

The 2021 monsoon brought the consequences into sharp focus. Flooding damaged homes and infrastructure and swept away farmland, apple trees and culturally significant objects. Three families sheltered elsewhere for three months before rebuilding uphill.

Yet the response was not simply to leave. Some residents adapted in place, while others moved uphill. Some could imagine relocating eventually but wanted to remain connected to Lubra. Those who moved remained tied to the village through livelihoods, farming and community relationships.

For residents, moving is therefore not simply about finding a safer place to build another house. It raises a deeper question: What happens when a community becomes separated from the landscape that has shaped its history, culture and way of life?

Climate risk does not create a simple choice between staying and leaving. Communities may adapt in place, move locally, diversify their livelihoods, migrate temporarily or relocate. These choices are shaped not only by physical risks, but also by livelihoods, resources, social ties and what people value about home.

What is lost when people move?

Resettlement can seem straightforward: identify a hazard, find safer land, rebuild houses and restore infrastructure. But a community is more than houses.

For Lubra’s Bon community, moving could mean leaving a monastery, agricultural land, memory-filled landscapes and a cultural setting that sustains identity. A new house can be built, but can a new place reproduce what made the old one home?

This does not mean communities should remain where risks are unacceptable or reject necessary resettlement. But safety cannot be the only measure of successful relocation. The question is whether people can rebuild meaningful lives in a new place, considering cultural continuity, spiritual spaces, land rights, livelihoods, social networks and intergenerational ties alongside infrastructure.

In Lubra, the question was not simply where people could go, but what they would leave behind.

Land and belonging

In Lubra, some households have moved uphill as flood risks increase. But safer ground does not always mean secure ownership. Some families have lost or seen farmland buried by floods while it remains registered in their names, leaving them liable for land taxes. Meanwhile, some new house plots lack Lalpurja , the official land-ownership certificate.

Families may escape physical danger yet remain uncertain about secure settlement.

Land is also governed through Gola Pratha in Lubra , a locally recognised allocation system lacking formal legal recognition. Resettlement is therefore about more than safer plots: ownership, land-use rights, customary systems and livelihoods shape lasting security.

The knowledge already exists

My conversations in Lubra challenged the assumption that climate knowledge must come from outside. Residents described changes in snowfall, rainfall, river behaviour and the landscape, knowledge built through generations of living with their environment.

Climate adaptation relies on hazard maps, technical assessments and infrastructure plans. These help measure physical risk but cannot capture everything. A hazard map can show flood exposure, but not what a monastery means to its community. A relocation plan can estimate rebuilding costs, but not the cultural cost of leaving a landscape.

Indigenous and local knowledge therefore cannot be an afterthought. Communities are not merely policy recipients; they are knowledge holders and participants in decisions about their futures.

Rethinking climate-induced mobility

The story of Lubra matters beyond Lubra. Nepal contributes only around 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet faces growing risks from floods, landslides, glacial lake outburst floods, droughts and heatwaves. As these risks intensify, migration, relocation and resettlement will become increasingly important to climate adaptation.

Moving people away from hazards can create new vulnerabilities. Mobility is rarely a simple move from unsafe to safe places. People may stay, adapt, move locally, migrate temporarily, diversify livelihoods or relocate. Choices reflect environmental risk alongside livelihoods, land rights, social networks and cultural ties.

(Left) Traditional Bon religious symbol representing the Bon faith. (Right) The newly reconstructed chorten, rebuilt on higher ground after the original was swept away by the 2019 flood./Prakriti Joshi

Where resettlement is necessary, rebuilding should consider land rights, livelihoods, cultural and spiritual spaces, social networks, customary institutions and community participation.

Lubra taught me that these answers cannot come only from maps or plans. They must begin with listening: where people feel safe, want to remain, and what they cannot afford to lose.

Himlung Himal avalanche: toll rises to 7; nine Nepalese workers and guides still missing

Three more bodies recovered on Wednesday after bad weather hampered Tuesday’s rescue effort

Avalanche struck base camp amid heavy rain and snowfall; Nepal still reeling from August flash floods

Three more bodies were recovered from Nepal’s Himlung Himal peak on Wednesday, 30 September, taking the death toll from Sunday’s avalanche to seven, with nine people still missing.

The avalanche struck the base camp of the 7,126-metre Himlung Himal in the Nar Phu area of Manang district, burying tents where 16 people, including mountain guides and support staff, had been sheltering.

Officials said all seven bodies recovered so far were of Nepalese nationals, as were the nine people still missing.

Rescue operations were hampered by bad weather on Tuesday but resumed on Wednesday, with teams recovering three more bodies.

A 14-member rescue team has been deployed to search for the missing workers and guides, who provide logistical and other support to climbing expeditions.

Around two dozen Nepali high-altitude workers and guides from Himalayan Holidays and Imagine Nepal Trek and Expedition had travelled from Kathmandu to Himlung Himal about two weeks ago to prepare for the climbing season.

publisher.title: News India Times

Sewa International (USA), based in Sugar Land, TX, plans to provide educational assistance to 10,000 children affected by the recent flash floods. It also plans to establish 10 skill development centers in flood-hit districts of Nepal to help people who lost their livelihoods, rebuild their lives.

Sewa USA President Srikanth Gundavarapu (third from left, top photo) with the Sewa Nepal team and children (bottom photo) during his visit to Nepal. ALL PHOTOS: Sewa International

Sewa USA’s President Srikanth Gundavarapu, who recently returned from a visit to the affected areas in Nepal, unveiled Sewa’s plans saying helping people rebuild their lives is Sewa’s priority, a press release from the organization said. The plan includes helping at least 500 families rebuild their homes, helping Nepali farmers restore their agricultural land, and providing mental-health assistance to help people cope with trauma.

Sewa announced $100,000 in aid immediately after the floods on August 26, and about 90 Sewa volunteers are actively involved in relief work. Sewa’s goal is to raise over $1 million for Nepal relief and as of September 30, it had reached 76% of its goal, the press release said.

- ADVERTISEMENT -

Returning from his two-day visit to Nepal’s flood-affected areas to assess the damage and get an overview of the ongoing relief work, Gundavarapu said he felt overwhelmed by the lives destroyed, families torn apart, and the death and mayhem caused by the floods. Gundavarapu and a team of volunteers from Sewa Nepal and other partner organizations traveled over 125 miles through the flood-hit communities. They met with affected families, local response teams, and government officials in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. The team saw homes washed away, roads and bridges destroyed, and communities cut off by mud, rocks, and debris. In some areas, temporary zip-lines helped residents cross rivers while connectivity was being restored. Thousands of children cannot attend school, and families are not able to see dear ones due to the dance of destruction caused by turbulent waters.

At the Sewa-run Janjati Kalyan Ashram hostel in Thepla, Nuwakot, the team found families who had lost family members, as well as a principal who continued to support over 800 children in her school, despite losing her home in the floods.

The stories and the extent of damage revealed the long road ahead for affected families and communities. “Sewa’s ongoing efforts are focused not only on immediate relief, but also on supporting children, education, rehabilitation, and rebuilding lives,” the organization said.

Working with Sewa Nepal and Nepal CMA (Community Medicine Assistant) Association, Sewa USA has distributed more than 800 grocery and hygiene kits and 700 shelter and medical kits. Sewa volunteers served more than 2,250 cooked meals during the first five days and continue to provide about 150 meals daily. More than 150 people received medical check-ups through health camps, while over 500 emergency lighting and power-support items were provided, including 200 units to the Nepal Police.

“Sewa USA invites individuals, community organizations, corporations, and foundations to support its Nepal Flood Relief and Rehabilitation efforts. Donations will help sustain immediate assistance and expand long-term programs focused on children, education, shelter, skills, and livelihoods, the press release said.

Donation Link: https://sewausa.org/NepalFlashFloodRelief

title: Remembering Suresh Raj Sharma, doyen of Nepal’s modern education - The Kathmandu Post
description: Remembering Suresh Raj Sharma, doyen of Nepal’s modern education  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
In the mid-1980s, as he hit his mid-40s, Professor Suresh Raj Sharma found himself questioning what exactly he was doing with his life. He had enjoyed opportunities rare even for a hill high-caste man with a middle-class background: a PhD in Chemistry from the United Kingdom; a full professorship at a age of 38 at Tribhuvan University; an array of appointments at elite government institutions, including the Council for Technical Education and Vocational Training; and an enviable network of diplomats, bureaucrats and educationists in a country where being ‘ aafno manchhe ’ ensured upward mobility. He was at the prime of his career, but something was amiss.

What followed is a story of institution-building in the midst of a country in transition. Thirty-five years after its establishment, Kathmandu University, which tapped into the aspirations of middle-class Nepalis for quality education, remains arguably the most successful public academic institution in Nepal. This was made possible with the primary vision and grit of Sharma, the founding vice-chancellor, who passed away on September 23, at the age of 86.

Tribhuvan University, the only university at the time, was imploding under the weight of its enormous responsibility to educate an entire country, compounding its struggle to navigate internal and external political dynamics. The end of the Panchayat regime was imminent as the struggle to restore democracy escalated. For Sharma, it was time for reinvention. It was at this moment that he met Sitaram Adhikary, Bhadra Man Tuladhar and Ramesh Nath Dhungel, individuals who had built fairly successful careers on the foundation of the old system but had a ‘common desire’ to do something more than just a job. They ended up establishing the Kathmandu Valley Campus in 1985, with significant support from Tribhuvan University, which not only waived the affiliation fee but also provided classrooms at the Institute of Engineering. Valley Campus quickly became one of the most sought-after academic institutions of the time, giving Sharma and his friends the confidence to turn it into a university. Kathmandu University was established in Dhulikhel, Kavre, about 30 kilometres east of Kathmandu, in 1991, as the first non-governmental university of a redemocratised Nepal.

This new university would compensate for the inadequacies of Tribhuvan University, which had struggled to catch up with the changed socio-political context—marked by a liberalised market economy, a growing aspiration among the people to climb the social ladder—and limit the exodus of students for higher education amid a perpetual state of underdevelopment. The political instability that became a permanent national character further pushed the aspirational class abroad, as TU and its affiliated campuses became sites of political struggle. Students always seemed to be out on the streets fighting the government of the day; teachers were busy teaching extra classes in private colleges to meet their daily expenses.

Meanwhile, KU offered students the opportunity others often couldn’t: innovative programmes, updated curricula, regular classes and timely exams. It also offered teachers a competitive salary that enabled them to remain on campus to teach and conduct research. It had little internal bureaucracy to stop teachers from securing research funding and international mobility. KU quickly gained the reputation of a stable, agile and cosmopolitan institution in a country where the general sentiment is “nothing works in this country!”

As the new university grew in its size and public profile, Sharma, the avant-garde , began to be identified as the torch-bearer of quality higher education in Nepal. Despite the enormous burden of managing resources for an ever-burgeoning university, he continued to find his way into the classroom to teach chemistry. Sangeeta Shakya, a Valley Campus alum who joined in 1985, remembers Sharma as a motivated teacher who taught students beyond the immediate subject. Shakya, who is now a professor of biotechnology at KU, says, “He was deeply concerned that the careers of the people who worked with him should grow, too, along with the university itself.”

Faculty and staff members who joined KU in its early days remember seeing Sharma happiest as he returned from his classes, often wearing a white apron. But as the university grew, his presence in the classes grew thinner. The devotion with which the faculty, staff and students helped build the university had now begun seeking a greater say in how it functioned. Beyond the university campus in the hills of Dhulikhel, the country was undergoing a churning, which impacted all walks of national life: the Maoist insurgency and the politicisation of public institutions. The national became the institutional, despite KU’s valiant attempts at maintaining its autonomy.

Those who have worked with Sharma attribute his success partly to his acute awareness of political dynamics and his ability to work with people across the political spectrum. But his acuity didn’t always work in his favour.

Sijan Baral, who started his career as an English faculty member and worked alongside Sharma, said the founding vice-chancellor preferred to work with a small circle of people, which proved quite effective in delivering results. But not everyone was happy with such an arrangement anymore. What was earlier known as Sharma’s circle began to be identified as a coterie. Discontent brewed, leading to protests for establishing unions of professors, staff and students. The university that Sharma and his friends nurtured with great care had outgrown them.

“Professor Sharma and his friends were shocked, even embarrassed, by the protests,” Baral said. “This was the first time they were facing resistance from within.” The stalemate ended with a nominal acknowledgement of the professor, staff and student councils as apolitical formations, only to be officialised over a decade later.

As the country entered a protracted period of transition, the university remained a site of political contestation, culminating in Sharma’s abrupt exit just a year into his sixth term, thereby bringing an abrupt end to his 21-year stint as vice-chancellor in 2012. In the years since he gave up the executive role to continue serving as the chair of the Board of Trustees, the university expanded rapidly, a departure from his more conservative approach of maintaining ‘a boutique university’, but his primary vision of quality education persisted.

There is no dearth of critics who claim Sharma remained attached to the university long past his prime. Others specify how he could have run it differently. But few question his moral authority, with “What would Suresh Sir say?” serving as a common reference point in the university’s decision-making even today.

In his last years, though, the magic of his moral authority seemed to wane as the relationship between the university and the Dhulikhel Hospital, its teaching hospital, soured. As the two entities diverged from their common path, the patriarch kept urging them to make amends, reminding them, in long, rambling monologues, of the efforts put to bring them into existence, and how the separation of these inalienable entities would be an affront to the town of Dhulikhel, which had helped establish them outside the periphery of the capital city by giving them a home.

Dhulikhel had given Sharma himself a home too—a home away from his ancestral Sindhuli and acquired Kathmandu, a family beyond his legal heirs. The day Sharma passed away, I asked Ambika, my colleague at the university, who has an A4-sized portrait of him pasted on her office pinboard, who Sharma was for her.

She said Sharma was a father figure more than anything else. Long before she began her career at the university as a receptionist, she overheard her father tell the founding vice-chancellor, “My family of five brothers will donate five ropani of our land to the university.” Within years, she saw classrooms grow on the terraces where her family grew maize and sesame. One of her brothers studied here, and another teaches here now; her son studies here, and her daughter attends the university’s high school.

“How will you remember him?” I pressed.

“I’ll remember him as the man who turned our makaibari into a global university,” she said.

title: Nepal’s disaster has laid bare the world’s adaptation accountability gap - Climate Home News
description: Nepal’s disaster has laid bare the world’s adaptation accountability gap  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
This is the first in a series of monthly columns from Climate Home News Editor Megan Rowling. They are exclusively available to Pro subscribers.

The deadly flash flood that thundered down Nepal's Bhote Koshi valley a month ago may have been hard to predict given the complexity of monitoring glacial slopes in the high mountains. But it should come as a surprise to no one that such a disaster could happen in a world set to barrel past the 1.5C warming limit governments agreed to in 2015.

I say this with confidence because even before the ink was dry on the Paris Agreement, former colleagues and I were writing extensively about the dangers posed by accelerating glacier melt in the Himalayas. I went back to look at what we covered, often working with local journalists in Pakistan, India and Nepal. It was substantial.

Comment: The response to Nepal’s disaster is a test for global climate institutions

In one story from a conference on climate change and geology, Bill McGuire, a professor who then led the Benfield Hazard Research Centre at University College London, was quoted as saying: “The most likely thing we are going to see soon is an increased level in giant landslides in mountainous terrains, huge collapses, millions of cubic metres of rock.”

That is precisely what unleashed Nepal’s most recent disaster, some 13 years later.

Other articles zoomed in on internationally funded programmes to prevent glacial lake outburst floods; studies warning of the rising risks to downstream communities; and cross-border efforts (or lack of them) to set up monitoring systems. But information has not led to sufficient action.

Falling behind intensifying impacts

Reporting on climate-related disasters over the past 20 years (it was way back then that UN aid chief John Holmes started referring to extreme weather as the “new normal”) has been a pretty frustrating beat, as things have gotten dramatically worse.

There’s no question that our understanding of the risks has grown hugely - alongside our knowledge of how to protect people and infrastructure in the face of fast-growing threats.

Yet governments and businesses have dragged their feet on adaptation policies and practical measures, even when confronted with the numbers showing it’s far cheaper to prevent and prepare than to clean up and rebuild after a flood or a storm. This intransigence has left a yawning chasm in the world’s ability to deal with climate change-driven impacts.

Let’s call it the adaptation accountability gap.

Sep 23, 2026 News UN Climate Summit: UN chief says world has tools to end fossil fuel age At the UN Secretary-General’s climate summit in New York, countries shared their energy transition plans while Nepal and island nations advocated for more international support Read more

Sep 24, 2026 News Threatened by rising seas, small islands secure right to keep their statehood Efforts to protect marine ecosystems and coastal communities have risen up the political agenda at the UN General Assembly in New York Read more

These days we see the effects all around us - in hospital emergency rooms where workers and older people struggle with heat exhaustion; in campsites and hotels abandoned by holidaymakers fleeing forest fires; in flooded streets piled high with mud, broken furniture and twisted cars.

The only bright side to the growing climate chaos we’re experiencing is that it’s become practically impossible for politicians and corporate bosses to ignore the evidence - and the rising cost to their balance sheets. Voters who can no longer afford to shoulder the economic and social burden of this damage need to let their leaders know time’s up.

1.5C overshoot means adapting differently

Last week, during Climate Week NYC, I moderated an event packed with experts who work on adapting to climate change - from Nepal to Brazil, from Sierra Leone to the Marshall Islands, and from communities to the top of governments and UN agencies. They spoke of tree-planting to stabilise slopes, heat insurance for informal workers, a climate risk guide for midwives, drought-resistant seeds and solar panels to irrigate farmland along the Nile.

Amid the diversity of experiences and approaches, there were two common threads: first, as underlined by the UN Environment Programme's new report on overshooting 1.5C, we may have missed the boat to catch up on adaptation as we know it.

With global warming continuing apace, we’ll need to come up with new “transformational” strategies if the coral reefs, ice sheets, oceans and other natural systems on which we rely cross tipping points and unleash cascading consequences. Nepal’s flash flood is being flagged as an example of the kind of disaster that requires a major change in how we think about adaptation.

Second, the investment required to adapt to intensifying climate shocks and stresses can no longer be seen as something to be squeezed out of shrinking foreign aid budgets. There are a growing number of tried-and-tested funds and mechanisms for channelling finance at the local, national and global levels - these must be filled, replenished and used without delay.

Businesses need to get stuck in too, not least to safeguard their assets, operations and profits - but also because in some sectors like agriculture or water there are opportunities for a return. Despite this, there are many activities governments will have no choice but to pay for, such as moving people out of the path of rising seas.

Finance not flowing where needed

Mikko Ollikainen, who heads up the UN’s pioneering Adaptation Fund for developing countries, told the event the fund has a portfolio of projects worth $1.6 billion but a pipeline waiting to be financed to the tune of $1.8 billion. Yet, in recent years, as needs balloon, donor nations have failed to meet its annual fundraising target of $300 million at COP climate summits.

The chair of the UN climate body for implementation, Julia Gardiner, said she expects to see more pressure on governments at November’s COP31 summit in Türkiye to show how they will meet a goal to triple adaptation finance by 2035 and fill the under-resourced coffers of the fledgling Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD).

Prakriti Dhakal, personal under-secretary to Nepal’s prime minister, speaks at an event on adaptation held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and moderated by Climate Home News, on September 24, 2026 in New York. (Photo@ Photo: Corinna Schutte / United Nations Foundation) Prakriti Dhakal, personal under-secretary to Nepal’s prime minister, speaks at an event on adaptation held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and moderated by Climate Home News, on September 24, 2026 in New York. (Photo@ Photo: Corinna Schutte / United Nations Foundation)

Nepal, meanwhile, is still waiting for a formal response to its request to the FRLD for urgent support to tackle the aftermath of the flood. Manjeet Dhakal, a Nepali scientist who advises least-developed countries in the UN climate process, said the disaster - which killed over 1,450 people and left nearly 6,000 missing - cannot be treated as just the latest climate crisis that grabs the headlines before it’s replaced by another.

That was backed up by Prakriti Dhakal, personal under-secretary to Nepal’s prime minister, who has been working closely on the emergency response. She said she had received many condolences and warm words of support during her meetings in New York.

But, she asked, “when you go home, will you continue having that sympathy for us that translates into something rational, something long-term, to strengthen the communities in Nepal?” A fitting response would be for governments to get behind a new Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, proposed by Nepal’s leader at the UN last week, as one way to start closing the adaptation accountability gap.

In Nepal, teachers mourn students who never returned

FLASH FLOODS: Across Rasuwa and neighboring districts, about 500 students and 24 teachers remain missing, while 18 schools have been damaged

AFP, RASUWA, Nepal

Add TT as Preferred Source



Each morning at a school in flood-ravaged Nepal, teachers taking attendance are served a painful reminder of the disaster as they mark in red the names of students who never came back.

The catastrophic flood, triggered by a glacial collapse near the China-Nepal border, on Aug. 26 killed more than 1,400 people, the majority in Nepal.

More than 5,000 remain missing in the Himalayan nation one month after the tsunami-like waves swept away roads, bridges and settlements in the mountainous regions up north.

A teacher instructs students at Neelakantha Secondary School in Rasuwa, Nepal, on Monday. Photo: AFP

At the Neelakantha Secondary School in hard-hit Rasuwa, a teacher marked red circles beside the names of children missing since the flood.

Unlike more than a dozen schools destroyed by the floods, the Neelakantha school, sitting on relatively higher ground, remained largely intact.

displayDFP('ad-IR1', 'm');

However, it lost 70 of its students and four teachers.

“If you look at Rasuwa, you can’t find a family that has not lost a family member,” principal Madhav Lamichhane said. “All the students and teachers are going through the same pain.”

Most of the missing Neelakantha pupils were on their way to the school from riverside settlements when floodwaters tore through the valley.

“We have been remembering our students with every breath,” said Rama Paudel, a 36-year-old teacher. “They have lost their lives in this disaster at such a young age. It’s a great loss.”

Across Rasuwa and neighboring districts, about 500 students and 24 teachers remain missing, while 18 schools have been damaged, with recovery costs estimated at up to US$15.47 million, Nepalese government data showed.

“This is the worst situation ever the education sector has experienced,” Nepalese Ministry of Education and Sports spokesman Shree Prasad Bhattarai said.

Initial assessments by UNICEF show learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children at 62 schools and learning centers across the flood-affected region.

“Education is a critical part of children’s recovery after a disaster,” UNICEF representative Alice Akunga said last week. “Returning to learning provides children with a sense of stability, routine and hope at a time when many have experienced significant loss and uncertainty.”

However, for many families, sending children back to school was not yet possible.

Fewer than half of Neelakantha Secondary School’s 508 students have resumed classes since lessons restarted two weeks ago.

Lamichhane said about 150 students were still unable to reach the school, because bridges and roads had been swept away.

Some classrooms have been repurposed as relief distribution centers, underscoring the challenges of restoring normalcy.

Teachers say psychological scars might prove even harder to overcome than damaged infrastructure.

“We have many students who do not have their parents or have seen their friends being swept away,” teacher Shiva Ram Bhatta said. “It has been a month now, but it is difficult for them to focus.”

Relief supplies are reaching many survivors, he said, but the next phase of recovery would require much more than food and shelter.

“We have enough relief materials,” he said. “Now we need psychosocial therapy and a permanent way out so that they can feel normal again.”

title: Nepal’s Climate Displaced Have No Place in the World’s Climate Debate - Everest Chronicle
description: Nepal’s Climate Displaced Have No Place in the World’s Climate Debate  Everest Chronicle
publisher.title: Everest Chronicle
full_article:
When Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah stood before the UN General Assembly on September 24 and invoked a "Himalayan Tsunami," he brought the world's attention to a mounting climate emergency. But behind the statistics and the demands for climate justice lay a quieter crisis: the climate-induced displacement of thousands of people who had lost not only their homes and livelihoods, but their place to return to.

That crisis began on August 26, when a catastrophic flood swept through the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli river corridor after an ice-and-rock collapse near the Nepal–Tibet border sent a wall of water and debris tearing through Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan districts. By September 21, Nepal's disaster authorities had recorded 1,451 deaths and 5,745 people still missing, among them 636 foreign nationals from 35 countries. The government's rapid damage and needs assessment put the disaster's damage and losses at roughly US$2.7 billion, with recovery needs approaching US$4.8 billion - close to a tenth of the country's entire GDP.

It was against this backdrop that Prime Minister Shah made his larger argument: that Nepal, despite its very small contribution to global greenhouse-gas emissions, should not be left to carry the financial consequences of a warming planet alone. It was, by any measure, a legitimate and necessary appeal.

Yet the timing exposed a harder truth. On that same day, as Shah addressed the UNGA, US President Donald Trump was hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House for a state visit. The leaders of the world's two superpowers, whose countries also account for the largest share of historical and current greenhouse gas emissions, spent that week trading niceties, negotiating trade deals and artificial intelligence, and managing strategic geopolitical relations, while a small Himalayan nation was still pulling bodies and searching for survivors out of the mud.

That juxtaposition: a state dinner over trade in Washington, and a plea for survival at the UNGA - is perhaps the clearest illustration of how vulnerable countries and their populations will fare as climate disruption intensifies. The world's great powers control a disproportionate share of global economic resources, technological capacity, energy systems and geopolitical influence. Their choices and decisions set the trajectory of the entire planet. Yet the human cost of climate change, and the failure of the international system to protect against it, falls on those least responsible for causing it. This asymmetry runs deeper than diplomacy.

The global climate debate has grown increasingly sophisticated about carbon, finance, adaptation, and loss and damage. Yet the people actually forced from their homes remain strangely peripheral to it. We tally destroyed bridges, damaged hydropower plants, and reconstruction costs. But the thousands of families who watched their homes vanish into the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli River are something more than a victim. They are the first visible wave of a legal and moral vacuum the world has spent decades avoiding: climate change now displaces people faster than international law has bothered to define them.

That vacuum is not an oversight so much as a design flaw. The 1951 Refugee Convention, still the only binding global instrument protecting displaced people, was built entirely around persecution - race, religion, nationality, political opinion, membership of a social group. It emerged from the ashes of the Second World War to give millions of stateless survivors a legal identity and a door to safety. But today's displacement doesn't necessarily look like the displacement of 1951. People are no longer only running from bullets and missiles; they are also running from rising water, from a collapsing mountain, from extreme heat, desertification and disappearing coastlines, among other forces.

Traditional refugee law, in other words, was designed for a 20th-century world in which the principal threats were governments, armies, political persecution and war. The 21st century is producing a different kind of displacement, driven by extreme climate events. But regardless of whether the perpetrator is a government or a changing climate, once a disaster destroys a person's ability to live safely, the humanitarian consequence is just as real.

Some international mechanisms already offer partial pathways. UNHCR recognizes that people displaced in the context of climate change and disasters may, in specific circumstances, have international protection claims. The Global Compact on Refugees similarly acknowledges that cross-border displacement can result from sudden-onset natural disasters and environmental degradation, while the 2018 Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration links climate change and human mobility, calling for adaptation and evacuation planning.

Still, these mechanisms remain fragmented, and a moral dilemma sits at their center: there is no universally recognized status called "climate-displaced person," and no global right to enter another country simply because one's home has been destroyed by climate catastrophe. The climate era demands that we think seriously, and urgently, about displacement and human rights protection in the face of environmental catastrophe.

The scale of the problem makes that urgency hard to ignore. The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre's most recent Global Report found that by the end of 2025, more than 82.2 million people were living in internal displacement worldwide, with nearly 13.6 million displaced specifically by disasters. In the prior year, disasters drove the overwhelming majority of new displacements, with 99.5 percent of them linked to climate-related extreme weather. South Asia is not a bystander to this trend; it is close to its epicenter.

The trajectory only deepens from here. The World Bank's Groundswell modelling projects that, without serious climate and development action, up to 216 million people could be forced to relocate within their own countries by 2050, with South Asia alone accounting for roughly 40 million. None of them will qualify for international legal protection under existing law, even as climate-induced displacement is projected to become one of the defining human consequences of climate change. As Ian Fry, a former UN Special Rapporteur on human rights and climate change, has put it plainly, people displaced by climate impacts simply "fall through the cracks" of legal protection, because no treaty or mandate was written with them in mind.

If the international community is serious about climate justice, then, it cannot stop at reconstruction financing. It needs a parallel and equally urgent conversation about climate mobility and protection for the climate-displaced. They must be given legal recognition, cross-border movement options for the most acute cases, and durable relocation support for those who cannot return, financed by the wealthy emitters whose emissions helped drive them from their homes. Loss and damage cannot mean only compensation and rebuilt infrastructure. It must also mean recognizing that some communities, uprooted by forces entirely outside their control, are unable or will never be able to go back. Sadly, the world currently has no plan for them.

What Nepal, and other climate-vulnerable countries, should demand is more than a bigger fund. They need a framework that formally recognizes climate-induced displacement as a distinct protection category, along with dedicated resettlement and residency pathways for when people cannot safely relocate within their own country. Major emitting nations should make binding commitments that go beyond one-time disaster payouts.
